identification.title: Holy Forever
identification.notes: Written by Chris Tomlin, Brian Johnson, Jenn Johnson, Jason Ingram and Phil Wickham. CCLI 7201044. The publisher lists Isaiah 6:3, Colossians 1:16 and Ephesians 1:20-23 behind it.

claims.structuralNotes: Two verses, a repeated chorus and a bridge. The chorus takes up the seraphim's cry; the bridge moves to the Lamb who was slain and the song the redeemed sing.

claims.claim: God is holy, and the heavenly host cry it without ceasing.
claims.subject: The holiness of God

claims.claim: God's name is above every other name.
claims.subject: The name of God

claims.claim: The Lamb who was slain is worthy of praise.
claims.subject: The atonement

claims.claim: The redeemed will sing this song without end.
claims.subject: Eternal worship

claims.claim: All creation was made by him and exists for him.
claims.subject: Creation

strengths.title: Takes its chorus from the seraphim, not from a sentiment
strengths.explanation: The central line is the cry of Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4 rather than a modern phrase about God's greatness. A congregation singing it is joining a text rather than inventing one.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts — the cry the chorus takes up.

strengths.title: Names the Lamb who was slain
strengths.explanation: The bridge grounds the holiness in the crucified Christ rather than leaving God's greatness abstract. It is the point where the song stops being general adoration and becomes Christian.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and wealth and wisdom.

strengths.title: Locates the singer inside a made world
strengths.explanation: The second verse says everything was made by him and for him, which places the congregation's praise within a creation that already belongs to God rather than as something they add.
strengths.scriptureRationale: All things were created through him and for him.

strengths.title: Praise placed on a timeline that outlasts the singer
strengths.explanation: The song says this praise continues without end and that the redeemed join it. It relativises the present service, which is a healthy thing for a congregation to be told.
strengths.scriptureRationale: A great multitude from every nation crying salvation belongs to our God.

theological.assessment: Modern worship doing what it does well. The chorus is the seraphim's cry rather than a fresh sentiment, the bridge grounds it in the Lamb who was slain, and the second verse places the congregation inside a creation that already belongs to God. Nothing here needs correcting. What it stops short of is saying what the Lamb's death accomplished — the fact is named, the effect is not.

strengths.title: Builds to the bridge, and the bridge is the best of it
strengths.explanation: The song's climax coincides with its strongest content rather than with its loudest moment. Form and doctrine point the same way, which is not always the case in this genre.

strengths.title: Two words a congregation keeps
strengths.explanation: The title phrase is short, repeated and easy to hold. A room has it after one hearing and carries it out of the building.

strengths.title: Joins a crowd rather than describing a feeling
strengths.explanation: The song places the congregation among the heavenly host and the redeemed. That is corporate by construction rather than by pronoun, and it works.

concerns.title: The bridge sits high and stays there
concerns.explanation: As with much of this catalogue, the emotional peak is written for a lead voice. Rooms manage the chorus and thin out through the bridge, which is where the strongest content is.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly published in B flat and C. The bridge is the demanding part; choose the key for that rather than for the verses, since the bridge carries the doctrine.

range.key: Commonly published in B flat and C
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The title phrase repeats heavily, and what repeats is a scriptural cry rather than a hook. Repetition used the way a refrain should be.
communal.assessment: Built for a room and shaped so its climax is also its best content. The one practical caution is the bridge, which sits high — and since that is where the Lamb is named, losing the congregation there costs more than usual.

strengths.title: Plain words for a large subject
strengths.explanation: Holiness, creation and the slain Lamb are all delivered without technical vocabulary. Nothing needs explaining before a congregation can mean it.

strengths.title: The object is never in doubt
strengths.explanation: Between the seraphim's cry and the Lamb, the song could not be sung to anyone else. That is worth more than it sounds in a genre where the addressee is often left open.

concerns.title: What the Lamb accomplished is left unsaid
concerns.explanation: The bridge names him as slain but never says what the death achieved. A hearer who knows fills it in; one who does not hears that a lamb died and is now praised, without being told why the two are connected.

clarity.assessment: Clear throughout, with an unmistakable object and no jargon. Its one gap is at the most important point: the Lamb is named as slain, and what that death did is left for the hearer to supply.

synthesis.summary: Modern worship doing what it does well: the chorus is the seraphim's cry rather than a fresh sentiment, the bridge grounds it in the Lamb who was slain, and the second verse places the congregation inside a creation that already belongs to God. Nothing needs correcting. What it stops short of is saying what the Lamb's death accomplished.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The seraphim's cry that the chorus takes up directly.
The slain Lamb declared worthy, which the bridge names.
All things created through him and for him, which the second verse states.
The multitude whose praise the song joins the congregation to.
